message.content: A mechanical water pump moves water uphill by converting rotational or reciprocating motion into pressure that forces water through a pipe against gravity. In a common piston pump, a handle or motor drives a piston up and down inside a cylinder. As the piston rises, it creates a partial vacuum, and atmospheric pressure pushes water up through an inlet valve into the cylinder. When the piston descends, the inlet valve closes and the water is compressed, forcing the outlet valve open so water flows into the discharge pipe leading uphill. Because the outlet valve prevents backflow, each stroke traps and pushes water higher, and repeated strokes build enough pressure to lift water to an elevation greater than the source. The height the water can climb depends on the pressure the pump generates, since each stroke must overcome both gravity and friction in the pipe. In this way, mechanical energy is steadily transformed into the potential energy of elevated water.
